about: Computer-aided Design is the Michaelmas half of the Part IA Drawing course in Cambridge's Engineering Tripos: an introductory lecture followed by self-paced tutorials and assessed tasks in a professional solid-modelling package (SolidWorks on the 2024-25 and 2025-26 syllabus pages; the 2026-27 guide says only commercial CAD software), with helpdesk support and scheduled marking sessions. It is coursework for standard credit, not an examined paper; the 2026-27 credit notice gives 3 submissions of 5 marks each (15 marks, qualifying 15). This guide explains the course and the CAD tools its syllabus lists; it does not invent a syllabus.
topics: What the CAD course is and how it is assessed

Further modelling tools: revolves, sweeps, patterns, surfaces, sheet metal, Toolbox and design tables
Animation, motion analysis and preparing for the marking sessions

notes.h: What the CAD course is and how it is assessed
notes.body:
Computer-aided Design (CAD) is the Michaelmas half of the Part IA Drawing course in the Cambridge Engineering Tripos; manual Engineering Drawing follows in Lent. It is a hands-on skills course in solid modelling, not a lecture course with an exam.

How it runs (from the department's pages)
- The 2026-27 Part IA guide says the Michaelmas focus is the basic functionality of commercial CAD software. The course opens with an introductory lecture, and you then work through tutorials and tasks before your scheduled marking sessions, using the helpdesk for help.
- The most recent syllabus pages that could be read (2024-25 and 2025-26) describe one lecture in week 1 of Michaelmas, a Tutorials sheet to work through, an assessed Tasks sheet, helpdesk support across the term and marking at three fixed sessions. Those pages name SolidWorks as the package. Check Moodle for the current year's software and dates.

Aims and objectives (paraphrased from the syllabus)
- Gain a working knowledge of solid modelling.
- Use a professional CAD package to model components and assemblies.
- Turn ideas, designs and real objects into CAD models in several ways.
- Produce outputs, including animations, that communicate ideas.

How it is assessed
- All Part IA coursework is for standard credit. The 2026-27 credit notice gives CAD 3 submissions worth 5 marks each: 15 marks in total, and the qualifying mark is also 15.
- Each submission earns its 5 marks for satisfactory effort. Marks are lost only if there are substantial gaps in the work despite the helpdesk support available.
- Raw coursework marks across Part IA are capped at their qualifying levels. You need to complete every activity to get the full qualifying mark, and shortfalls reduce your coursework total, which counts in the Tripos total.

Why it matters beyond the marks
- The Design Challenge syllabus notes that its coursework may draw on IA CAD, so the skills are used again within the year.
- Modelling a part in CAD and then drawing it by hand in Lent reinforces the same ideas of views, sections and dimensions.

Exam tips: there is no written exam on CAD. Treat each marking session as the deadline, have every task complete and saved before you arrive, and use the helpdesk early rather than the night before.

notes.h: Core workflow: sketches, parts, assemblies and drawings
notes.body:
Almost everything in a parametric solid modeller such as SolidWorks follows the same workflow. Getting it right makes the later tasks much easier.

Sketches
- A part starts with a 2D sketch on a plane (front, top or right) or on a flat face of the model.
- Geometry is controlled by relations (for example horizontal, coincident, tangent, equal) and by dimensions.
- In SolidWorks the sketch colour shows its state: blue for under-defined, black for fully defined, and red for over-defined, where relations or dimensions conflict.
- Aim to fully define sketches so that the model changes predictably when you edit a dimension.

Features and parts
- A feature turns a sketch into 3D: an extruded boss adds material and an extruded cut removes it. Fillets and chamfers are applied to existing edges.
- The FeatureManager design tree records features in order. Later features depend on earlier ones, so plan the order and name important features.
- Design intent means building the model so it behaves as the designer wants when dimensions change. For example, dimension a hole from the edge that matters for assembly and use symmetry where the part is symmetrical.
- Assign a material so the software calculates correct mass properties (otherwise it uses a default density).

Assemblies
- An assembly brings parts together. In SolidWorks the first component inserted is fixed by default.
- A free rigid body has six degrees of freedom: three translations and three rotations. Mates remove them.
- Standard mates include coincident, parallel, perpendicular, tangent, concentric, distance and angle. For example, a concentric mate between a pin and a hole leaves the pin free to slide along and rotate about the shared axis.
- Leave intended motion free (for a mechanism) and fully constrain everything else.

Drawings
- Drawings are generated from the part or assembly and stay linked to it, so changes to the model update the drawing.
- Place standard views, add section and detail views, and insert dimensions and annotations. The same conventions you meet in the Lent manual-drawing course apply, such as projection method, line types and dimensioning rules.

File types in SolidWorks
- .SLDPRT for parts, .SLDASM for assemblies and .SLDDRW for drawings. An assembly refers to its part files rather than containing them, so keep all files together when you move or submit work.

Exam tips: if a model rebuilds with errors after an edit, look at the earliest failing feature in the tree first. Errors cascade downwards, and fixing the first one often clears the rest.

After parts, assemblies and drawings, the syllabus lists tools for more complex shapes and for efficient modelling: revolving, sweeping, repeated patterns, surfaces, sheet metal, the toolbox of standard parts and design tables. Below is what each one does in a modeller like SolidWorks, the package named on the 2024-25 and 2025-26 syllabus pages.

Revolve
- A sketch profile is rotated about an axis (a centreline, line or edge) to make an axisymmetric solid, such as a shaft, pulley or bottle.
- The profile must not cross the axis. You can revolve through less than 360°.

Sweep
- A profile is moved along a path to make shapes such as pipes, handles and springs.
- You need two sketches: the profile and the path. The profile is usually drawn on a plane at the start of the path. A guide curve can be added to vary the shape along the way.

Patterns and mirrors
- A linear pattern repeats a feature along one or two directions; a circular pattern repeats it around an axis; a mirror reflects it about a plane.
- Patterning the feature, rather than modelling each copy, keeps design intent: edit the original (the seed) and all copies update.

Surfaces
- Surface features have no thickness. They are useful for complex, flowing shapes that are hard to build from solid features.
- Surfaces can be joined (knitted) and thickened, or used to cut a solid, to turn them into a solid model.

Sheet metal
- Sheet metal parts are modelled with a uniform thickness and bends, for example a base flange, then edge flanges and tabs.
- The model can be flattened to give the flat blank needed for manufacture.
- The flat length depends on how the material stretches at each bend. This is set with a bend allowance or a K-factor. The K-factor locates the neutral axis as a fraction of the thickness from the inside face. For a bend through angle θ (in radians) with inside radius R and thickness T, the bend allowance is θ(R + KT).

Toolbox
- SolidWorks Toolbox is an add-in library of standard parts, such as bolts, screws, nuts, washers and bearings. You choose a standard part and size instead of modelling it, which saves time and keeps hardware consistent.

Design tables
- A design table is an embedded spreadsheet that sets the values of chosen dimensions (and can suppress features) for a list of configurations. One model can then represent a whole family of sizes, such as a range of brackets or bolts.

Exam tips: when a task asks for a family of parts or repeated features, a design table or a pattern is usually the efficient route, not separate models. Using the right tool is quicker and less error-prone.

notes.h: Animation, motion analysis and preparing for the marking sessions
notes.body:
The last part of the syllabus covers bringing assemblies to life and checking how they move. It also helps to have a clear plan for the three marking sessions.

Animating objects
- In SolidWorks, motion is set up in a motion study on a timeline below the model.
- There are three study types. Animation moves components by keyframes or motors without considering physics. Basic Motion gives an approximate simulation that accounts for things such as mass, gravity, springs and contact. Motion Analysis is a more accurate kinematic and dynamic analysis, available through the SOLIDWORKS Motion add-in in the more advanced licences.
- A motor (rotary or linear) drives a component at a set speed. The mates you defined decide how the rest of the mechanism follows. This is why correct mates matter: a mechanism with a missing mate will fly apart or lock up.
- An animation can be saved as a video file to communicate how a design works. The course aims explicitly include producing outputs such as animations.

Analysing motion
- Once a mechanism moves, you can trace the path of a point and plot quantities such as displacement, velocity or acceleration against time (the plotting tools are part of Motion Analysis).
- This links to Part IA Mechanics: for example, you can compare the velocity of a slider in a modelled slider-crank with a hand calculation.

Preparing for the marking sessions
- Read the Tasks sheet early and note what must be shown at each session.
- Work through the Tutorials sheet first. The tasks assume you can use the tools it introduces.
- Fully define sketches and mate assemblies properly. A well-constrained model is easier to edit, to debug and to demonstrate working.
- Save regularly, keep parts, assemblies and drawings in one folder, and check that files open on another machine before a session.
- Use the helpdesk as soon as you are stuck. The credit notice says marks are lost only for substantial gaps despite helpdesk support, so getting help in good time protects your marks.
- Missing a marking session or failing to submit costs coursework credit, so follow the department's procedure for rearranging coursework if you are ill.

Exam tips: the skills are judged by whether each task is complete and works. Spend your time on finishing every task to a sound standard rather than polishing one.

questions.q: In SolidWorks, a sketch turns red after you add a dimension. What does this indicate?
options: The sketch is over-defined, with conflicting relations or dimensions
questions.why: Red marks an over-defined sketch where a dimension or relation conflicts with others. Fully defined geometry is black and under-defined geometry is blue; extruding a sketch does not change its colour to red.

questions.q: A pin is mated into a hole with a single concentric mate. How many degrees of freedom does the pin still have relative to the hole?
questions.why: A concentric mate keeps the axes aligned, removing four of the six degrees of freedom and leaving translation along and rotation about the shared axis: 2. Zero would need further mates (for example a coincident face mate and a fixed angle) and describes a fully fixed pin. Four comes from thinking a concentric mate removes only the two sideways translations, forgetting that it also stops the pin tilting about the two axes perpendicular to the hole. Six is the count for a free body and ignores the mate altogether.

questions.q: You need a bracket in five sizes that differ only in a few dimensions. Which tool is designed for this?
questions.why: A design table drives chosen dimensions for multiple configurations of one model. A sweep makes a shape along a path, a circular pattern repeats a feature around an axis, and knitting joins surfaces; none of these creates a family of sizes.
